newsitem.title: EGYPT: Libya opposition says eight executed not U.S. spies.
newsitem.headline: Libya opposition says eight executed not U.S. spies.

text.p: A Libyan opposition group said on Saturday six senior army officers executed in Libya had taken part in a failed revolt against Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and that their death was meant as a warning to other rebels.

Libyan state radio said the six officers and two civilians were executed on Thursday after a Libyan military court found them guilty of spying using equipment supplied by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).

But the National Front for the Salvation of Libya, which operates mainly out of London, said in a faxed statement that Gaddafi ordered the men killed because they had taken part in an attempt by the army to overthrow him in October 1993.
"These accusations by the Libyan regime of spying and working for a foreign power will not hoodwink anybody or be believed by anybody," the NFSL said.

"We have no doubt that since the October revolution, Gaddafi has been waiting for the right time to take revenge on the men (who took part)...and we know for a fact these executions are meant to spread awe and dread into the souls of the opposition."
They said that an attempt on Gaddafi's life in August had contributed to the decision to execute the men who it said were jailed since 1993.

The convicted officers were identified as Colonel Muftah Muhammad Gharoum, Staff Colonel Mustafa Abu al-Qasim Massud, Flight Lieutenant-Colonel Saad Salah Faraj, Major Khalil Salim Muhammad, Major Ramadan al-Ihumi Muhammad Ali and Major Mustafa Hubayl al-Fudhil.
The two civilians were Misbah Saad Musbah and Sulayman Ghayth Muftah.
Libyan radio also said they had been accused of belonging to a banned opposition group and televised footage implied that they had been spying for the United States.
In Washington, U.S. officials dismissed the trial as a propaganda ploy and the human rights watchdog Amnesty International said the executions were an outrage.
